title: Festivals around the world: seven short texts
texts: The programme promises a dozen bands on three stages, but those who return every summer remember something else: tents pitched in a muddy meadow, queues for the showers, and conversations with strangers at three in the morning. Few people sleep more than a couple of hours, and almost everybody leaves hoarse and exhausted, planning next year's trip before they reach home.

For a few days each year, the ordinary rules seem to be suspended. Performers wear elaborate disguises of feathers, glitter and glass beads, and parade through the streets to the sound of drums. Because faces are hidden, a bank manager can dance beside a bus driver without either being recognised, and differences of status are forgotten. Whole neighbourhoods prepare the colourful costumes for months.

As darkness settles over the water, people kneel at the edge and release small paper boats, each carrying a candle and a wish. The current slowly spreads them into a glowing carpet. Nobody speaks; the only sound is the soft plash of the water, and the silence is part of the ceremony. Locals say that the flames that vanish around the bend carry sorrows away.

Wherever there is a fair, there are stalls, and at a food festival they are the main attraction. Visitors try regional dishes cooked over open fires, hand-made cheese and sweets prepared from recipes that grandmothers once guarded as secrets. Cooks compete for prizes, and judges, thanks to their experience, can taste the difference between a family recipe and a copy.

At the beginning of spring, crowds gather in the squares to throw handfuls of bright powder at one another. Within minutes everyone, from small children to elderly neighbours, is covered in red, yellow and pink, with faces like painted masks, and it becomes impossible to tell a friend from a stranger. Old quarrels are forgotten as laughter spreads, and stained clothes are worn as a badge of honour for days.

In many farming regions the end of the autumn work is marked by a ceremony in which the first loaves and baskets of fruit are carried to the church or the open field. People express gratitude for a good yield, or ask for better luck next year, and then share a meal at long tables. Traditional songs are sung, some of them older than the village itself.

As the clock approaches midnight, the whole city turns its eyes upward. Rockets burst above the rooftops, trailing sparks of gold and silver, and every street lights up as the crowds count down the final seconds before shouting greetings to the unknown people around them. Some families prefer to watch from windows, but most feel that the moment is better shared.
discuss: Which of these festivals would you most like to visit? Why?
What is the biggest festival or celebration in your town or region?
Why do people all over the world enjoy festivals?
